documentation.range:
This species is natively endemic to southern Europe. Its native European range encompasses most of Italy except the northern mountains, the east Adriatic coast of Croatia and Slovenia and southern Bosnia-Herzegovina, and many islands, among them Sicily (including an introduced population in the Aeolian Islands) and Sardinia (Speybroeck et al. 2016). The species ranges from sea level up to 2,200 m asl, but the species is usually found below 1,000 m asl (Speybroeck et al. 2016).

The species has been widely introduced within the European region: Cyprus (although the species is not mentioned by Baier et al. 2013), France (southern mainland France: Toulon, Château d'If, Hyères) and Corsica, Portugal (Lisbon), Spain (Balearic Islands (Menorca and southern Mallorca) and mainland Spain (historically in Santander and Almeria, and more recently Cantabria and Barcelona), and Montenegro (Speybroeck et al. 2016). An island subpopulation on Santo Stefano in the Eastern Pontine Islands (Italy) appears to have been introduced in the early 20th Century, and its occurrence on nearby Ventotine may result from an earlier introduction (Senczuk et al. 2018, 2019). Introduced subpopulations in Great Britain and mainland Greece have successfully been eradicated within three years of their introduction (Hodgkins et al. 2012, Adamopoulou and Pafilis 2019).

The species has also been introduced outside the European region, to North Africa (Tunisia, Libya), Türkiye (where it is found on both sides of the Bosporus), Russia (Tuniyev et al. 2020), and the United States (Speybroeck et al. 2016). In the Caucasus, Podarcis siculus campestris (De Betta, 1857) was introduced to the Black Sea coast (Sochi, Russia) (Tuniyev et al. 2020) and the Caspian coast (Baku, Azerbaijan) (Iskenderov et al. 2021).
documentation.population:
This is a very common species except in the northern part of its range. In some places it is an aggressive invasive species. It is known to outcompete native wall lizards in parts of its introduced European range (Speybroeck et al. 2016). Overall, its population - including introduced populations - is probably increasing, and in its native range is presumably at least stable.

In the Caucasus, subpopulations continue to increase in numbers and pose a danger to native rock lizards (Darevskia spp. - I. Doronin pers. comm. October 2022).
documentation.habitats:
The species is found in grassy areas, roadside verges, hedgerows, scrubland, woodland edges, inside pine plantations, vineyards, orchards, meadows, coastal dunes, parkland, urban areas, and on stone walls and buildings. In the northern part of its range, it mainly lives in riparian or coastal areas. It thrives in habitats disturbed by human activities, being common around human habitations and in gardens (Speybroeck et al. 2016). It favours mesic habitats and is replaced by other species in more arid, harsher environments (Speybroeck et al. 2016). It is an egg-laying species, with females laying up to four clutches a year each of 2-8 eggs (Speybroeck et al. 2016).

In the Caucasus it reaches high abundances in biotopes heavily modified by humans in urban areas (I. Doronin pers. comm. October 2022).
documentation.threats: There are no major threats to this adaptable species. In the northern part of its range, it is threatened by small scale agricultural conversion of its riverine habitats. Localised or insular subpopulations may be vulnerable by predation by cats, but generally it is an invasive that can displace native populations of other species in its invasive range (the southern part of its range and in the areas where it has been introduced). Its introduction is believed to be responsible for the loss of the Aeolian wall lizard from larger islands within that species' range (Speybroeck et al. 2016). It has been found to exhibit signs of population stress and reduced reproductive success in agricultural areas of Italy where it is exposed to "conventional" levels of pesticide treatment (Simbula et al. 2021a,b).
documentation.measures: It is listed on Annex II of the Bern Convention and Appendix IV of the EU Habitats Directive. It is protected by national legislation in a number of its range states. It occurs in many protected areas. Further research is needed to clarify its taxonomy.
documentation.use_trade: Because it is locally common, this species is collected for use as food for pet snakes. It has been introduced widely in part from animals included in the pet trade (e.g. to the United States, Kolbe et al. 2012).
documentation.rationale:
Global and European regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)
EU 27 regional assessment: Least Concern (LC)

This species is native-endemic to the European region. It is assessed as Least Concern globally and for the EU 27 Member States in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a broad range of habitats, large population, and because the population is stable or increasing.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Senczuk et al. (2019) proposed recognizing the mtDNA divergent Western Pontine lineage of P. siculus (a recognized species complex in which they suggest diversity may have been underestimated) as a distinct species, for which the name Podarcis latastei is available.

Speybroeck et al. (2020) recommended refraining from adopting this scheme pending nuclear DNA research and a fuller revision of this likely species complex. In a response to this arrangement Castiglia et al. (2021) pointed out that nuclear data had previously been reported by Senczuk et al. (2018) and was consistent with patterns between "accepted species pairs" of Podarcis. Castiglia et al. (2021) further supported an argument for species status by pointing to consistent morphological differences and an estimated divergence date of 4 million years ago.
